title: Streams: stdin, stdout, stderr
lead: Every Linux command has three standard channels: input, output and error. Understanding them is the foundation of redirection and pipes.
objectives: You tell stdin (0), stdout (1) and stderr (2) apart.
You redirect output and errors to files with `>`, `>>` and `2>`.
You merge or discard streams with `2>&1` and `/dev/null`.

sections.title: The three standard channels
body: A running program has three open channels: **stdin** (0) reads input, **stdout** (1) writes the normal result, **stderr** (2) writes error messages. By default input comes from the keyboard, output and errors go to the screen.
Because both land on the same screen they look mixed, yet they are separate channels. That separation lets you send errors to their own file.

commands.why: Reads a file and feeds the channel.

commands.what: When asked to list a missing path, the error goes to stderr.
commands.why: The message appears on screen but is not on stdout.

sections.tip: Channel numbers: 0 = input, 1 = output, 2 = error. You use them in redirections.

sections.title: Redirecting to files
body: `>` writes stdout to a file and **truncates** it. `>>` **appends**. `2>` redirects only stderr. `<` feeds a file as stdin.

If output and errors should go to the same file write `> file 2>&1`: stdout goes to the file first, then stderr is attached to wherever stdout goes. Order matters. `/dev/null` is a special file that discards everything written to it.

commands.what: Writes stdout to a file; an existing file is emptied.
commands.why: You keep the result for later.

commands.what: Appends stdout to the end of a file.
Writes only error messages to a file.
commands.why: Output stays on screen, errors are saved.

commands.what: Makes a file the command's input.
commands.why: Reads from a file instead of the keyboard.

commands.what: Sends stderr to wherever stdout goes.
commands.where: To collect everything in one file.
commands.why: Output and errors are saved together.

sections.tip: Safe habit: decide first whether you need `>>` or `>`. A wrong `>` silently wipes an existing file.
sections.warn: `>` empties the target file before the command runs. `sort file > file` destroys the file's content.

t01.text: Write text to the screen (stdout) with `echo hello`.
t01.hint: The output appears directly on screen.

t02.text: Print the file's content to stdout with `cat lab/names.txt`.

t03.text: List the missing path `lab/missing.txt` with `ls` and read the error message.

t04.text: Write the text to the file `out.txt` with `echo hello > out.txt`.
t04.hint: You see no output; check with `cat out.txt`.

t05.text: Append a second line to the same file with `echo world >> out.txt`.

t06.text: Put the error into `errors.txt` with `ls lab/missing.txt 2> errors.txt`.
t06.hint: The error no longer shows on screen.

t07.text: Feed the file as stdin with `cat < lab/names.txt`.

t08.text: Predict: when `ls lab/missing.txt > result.txt` runs, does the error appear on screen? Is `result.txt` filled? Run it to verify.
t08.hint: `>` redirects stdout only; the error is on stderr.

t09.text: Predict: what does `cat lab/names.txt | wc -l` print? Run it to verify.
t09.hint: `wc -l` counts lines; how many lines does the file have?

t10.text: Debug: `ls lab missing_dir > all.txt` prints the error on screen and it does not reach `all.txt`. Make `all.txt` contain both the listing and the error.
t10.hint: Add `2>&1` at the end of the command.

t11.text: Mini project: build `build.log`. 1) `echo start > build.log` 2) `ls lab >> build.log` 3) `ls nothing 2>> build.log`. The file must have 3 lines.
t11.hint: The first uses `>`, the others `>>` and `2>>`.

t12.text: Challenge: discard the errors of `ls lab missing_dir` into `/dev/null` and save the normal output to `found.txt`.

t13.text: Ticket: the auditor wants the number of users in `lab/names.txt` in `~/count.txt` (number only).
t13.hint: `wc -l < file` prints the count without a file name; save with `>`.

vm.intro: These commands run in your VM's home directory and only write files you create yourself; still, do not reuse the name of an important file.

v01.title: Separate output and errors
v01.text: List an existing file and a missing path; write output and errors to separate files, then show both.

blocks.cmd:
ls /etc/hostname /nonexistent > out.txt 2> err.txt
cat out.txt err.txt
blocks.expected:
/etc/hostname
ls: cannot access '/nonexistent': No such file or directory

differs: The error text varies slightly by distribution and language; `nonexistent` must appear.
If `out.txt` is empty, `/etc/hostname` does not exist on your system; use `/etc/hosts`.

v02.title: Overwrite and append
v02.text: Create a file with `>`, append a line with `>>` and show the result.
differs: If only `line two` appears you used `>` in both commands.

v03.title: Silence errors
v03.text: List a directory you cannot read as a normal user together with a file; discard the errors to `/dev/null`.
differs: If `hostname` is missing your system has no such file; as long as no error message appears on screen it worked.

q2.q: What does `echo x > file` do when the file already exists?
q2.explain: `>` truncates the file; use `>>` to append.

q3.q: Which command saves errors to a file and keeps normal output on screen?

options: It discards everything written to it
q4.explain: `/dev/null` is a black hole: whatever you write there vanishes.

summary: `>` overwrites, `>>` appends, `2>` redirects errors, `<` supplies input.
`2>&1` merges errors into output; order matters in `> file 2>&1`.

glossary.meaning: Standard input, channel 0; keyboard by default.
Standard output, channel 1; screen by default.
Connecting a channel to a file or another channel.
Special file that discards what is written.
